summary:
Kayseri stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring recorded roughly 313 violations across the country, about two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions and a documented rise in attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. A visitor in Kayseri faces this regime in the same way as anywhere else in Turkey, with the additional exposure that any checkpoint or hospital interaction can place identity documents and presentation in direct comparison.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, require permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose healthcare professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison, with trans people receiving care deemed illegal facing up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it. Human Rights Watch warned the measure would drive treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. The draft had not been reported as passed, but authorities have acted against LGBT people as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's review of 2025 found hostility converted into explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The same review counted six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the prior year, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Kayseri itself appears in the record through the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate, whose circular added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 followed, barring hospitals from recording the "other" option and requiring e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care in the province.

Street-level enforcement elsewhere in Turkey indicates what document checks entail. In 2025 police in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement preceded the passage of the law being invoked. Foreign nationals stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreigners to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated demands for an independent investigation came from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
The Erdoğan government's stated justification for these measures is the protection of "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. That framing gives enforcement a policy warrant even where the underlying statute has not been enacted, which is the pattern rights monitors describe through 2025.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the depth of the regime rather than as a statement of current law.

Comparatively, the draft package's treatment of gender-affirming care would place Turkey well outside the access norms of Council of Europe states, and the pending status of the draft has not delayed its use as a reference point in official rhetoric. The opposition of the Turkish Medical Association is the clearest institutional counterweight recorded in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kayseri seeking transition-related care face the medical-board route defined by the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, under which "gender reassignment" is an official reason for board reports, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requiring e-reports and removing the "other" option from hospital records. The practical effect on appointment availability and on how patients are recorded in provincial systems is not documented in the sources.

For LGBT residents nationwide, 2025 brought "Year of the Family" directives to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ association with criminal cases against 11 members, cancellation or banning of artistic events, 89 recorded torture or ill-treatment violations, and 540 freedom-of-expression violations. Detention decisions numbered 299 for the year.

Detainees and prisoners face placement by registered sex, arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, disrupted visits through transfers, and complaint mechanisms that are ineffective and can invite further violence. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 and the parliamentary intervention of 12 December 2025 show that these conditions were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No criminal charge, prosecution, court decision or enforcement action specific to Kayseri appears in the sources behind this record beyond the Provincial Health Directorate circular. Whether police in Kayseri conduct GBT-style identity checks, and how frequently, is not sourced.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and had not been reported as passed at that date. Its current legislative status, and whether any equivalent provision has since been enacted, remains unresolved in these sources.

The operational consequences of the Kayseri circular and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation for individual patients in the province, including any documented refusal of care, are not sourced. Nor is the effect of the regulation on wait times or on the availability of surgical referral.

Statistics on anti-trans violence in Kayseri specifically, and on the province's hate-crime recording practice, are not available in the inventory; the national figures cited are country-wide totals without provincial breakdown.
